questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between the `<b>` tag and the `<strong>` tag in HTML5, and why does this distinction matter for screen readers?
questions.a: `<b>` only applies bold styling without conveying importance, while `<strong>` indicates strong importance/emphasis semantically. Screen readers announce `<strong>` content with emphasis (changed tone/volume) but treat `<b>` as plain text. A wrong answer (e.g., "they do the same thing") reveals the student confuses visual presentation with semantic meaning — a critical error for accessibility questions in board exams.

questions.q: A student writes `<section><article>Blog Post</article></section>` and another writes `<article><section>Blog Post</section></article>`. Both render identically in browsers. Which is semantically correct for a standalone blog post, and why?
questions.a: `<article><section>...</section></article>` is correct because `<article>` represents a self-contained composition (the blog post), while `<section>` groups thematic content *within* it. Reversing them implies the section contains the article, violating the "article is independent" principle. A wrong answer shows the student doesn't grasp hierarchical semantics — a common board exam trap in case-based questions.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Using `<div>` and `<span>` with CSS classes is just as good as semantic tags because they look identical in browsers." Defend or refute with three technical arguments.
questions.a: Refute. (1) Accessibility: Screen readers navigate by landmark roles (`<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`) — `<div>` has no role. (2) SEO: Search engines weight `<h1>`–`<h6>`, `<article>`, `<header>` higher for content hierarchy. (3) Maintainability: Semantic tags self-document structure; `<div class="header">` requires reading CSS/HTML to understand intent. A student agreeing reveals they prioritize visuals over standards — a mark-losing error in board exam "justify" questions.
